title: Best Setup for Daily AI-Assisted Game Development Without Hitting Usage Limits?
author: AgeComfortable5104
selftext:
I’d like to spend a few hours coding my isometric RPG every day. For now, I bought a Codex subscription, but even after relatively simple requests, I managed to burn through my entire usage limit in less than two hours.

I’m considering getting a Claude subscription as well, possibly one of the higher-tier plans, and switching between Codex and Claude while working on the same project.

What would be the best setup if I want to work on my game consistently every day without constantly running into usage limits? Right now it’s pretty frustrating that I can only get a few hours of work done once a week before my limit is gone. :C

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I’m also using Codex (on a plus sub) so here is some of my own experience for you to consider.

The limits are way down right now, and also there is something weird going on. Keep an eye on the Codex reddit but don’t believe everything you see. There’s a lot of angry and confused people right now.

The choice of model is really important and you need to be sensible with which one you use. The meta is to use Sol to plan/orchestrate and then Luna to implement. The top level Sol Ultra and Max models do all sorts of things to give the best possible outcome but they don’t care about token use at all.

I’ve found Sol overthinks severely and Luna can churn for ages without getting a good result. My current setup is Sol Medium as the orchestrator and then it has a list of different roles it can call as sub agents with Luna, Terra or Sol depending on the task.

You have to stay active in the loop. If you throw a huge prompt (or a vague prompt) and then walk away then you will get a pile of burnt tokens and not much else. Have the orchestrator come back to you to approve the plan, then again when implementation is complete to approve the work. Don’t trust the agent’s own tests, your eyeballs are the final judge of success.

Work in small steps. Use a task system (I use backlog.md). Use GitHub so you can roll back easily. The further you go from a checkpoint the more risk you take of context drift.

Writing code is very expensive, talking about what you want is relatively cheap, sitting and thinking for a bit is free. Take the time to consider your game and what you want to happen. Take care to write clear instructions or documents. Take the time to read and correct what Codex outputs.

At the end of the day, $20 a month is hobby money so you need to be realistic about what you get for that. If I can get 20+ hours “on project” in a week then I’m doing ok. That isn’t Codex run time, that is time with me working in concert with Codex.

replies.author: DowntownNoLonger
replies.body:
Your model selection needs to reflect the task. 

You don't need a frontier model to import sprites. What you need is a sprite importing tool, planned by sol and implemented through Luna. 

Then you never need to use AI again for that task. 

You have to start thinking like an engineer running a software company instead of just a dude with solo dev working for you. 

Break everything in your studio down into tasks. Sprite importing -> tool. 
Object database -> tool. 
Coding work -> Sol planner, Luna implementor. 
Quest System -> tool

Build your studio using the agents. Use agents when you need code, fresh art, planning documents, etc. 

Also, the above suggestions is right on the money. 

Spend expensive reasoning doing just that -> reasoning and planning. Then you can go a lot cheaper in implementation. 

Every repeated task ask this question: Can this be done by a deterministic tool or an agent skill?

Build your tools so that the cheapest model can run them, if you like. 

Save money and context on by building a master_index.md file for your repo. A substantial map with all files, general notes and dependencies they rely on. Tell your Sol planner to use the map on the slices they are working on. 

The overall suggestion is the same though, think like a systems engineer and build a studio instead. 

Once all that's done, you can then increase productivity, lower costs, and produce many games and projects for cheap.

comments.author: Morphid
comments.body: Subagents, your primary agent or “supervisor” should be the cheapest dumbest model (Gemini) then work your way up from that depending on the need of the subagent, it should only have the ability to spawn subagent. My technical director runs opus or fable, programmer opus or sonnet, qa opus, have ai research the best one for the assigned task and utilize free/dumb models as much as possible. Also include research agents or workflows to go investigate best practices and document and index them prior to starting a new area (3d modeling, textures, design, game philosophy, etc) add in the docs and have them indexed for token saving. Use things like context7 mcp to easily look up docs first via index rather than a web search. Order should be local->c7->web

replies.author: work_in_marketing
replies.body:
I think the three main causes:

- Long threads creates a lot of context.
- Higher tier model on max effort costs more tokens.
- Multiple sessions running at the same time.

The last one is a big one. To avoid file conflicts you can have each session plan out the whole task and the code before getting your approval to apply it to the project. So the real limit becomes your metal ability to context switch.

As examples, you can have one session play through your game to find bugs. Another session generates 20 different mockups of a UI card you want. A third session is doing in depth research on how the competitors solved X. Session 4-6 are solving tasks on your todo list. A seventh session is where you brainstorm future tasks.

It's cool to see the power in motion but it probably isn't sustainable. I'm mostly doing 1-3 sessions nowadays. I do however believe that people could utilize it more because I often see people just sit and wait for the response or have it as an excuse to scroll Reddit.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
Research ways to be more token efficient.  Stuff like caveman or rtk.  /compact.  I heard that if your context window gets over 60% the pricing per token increases.  

I've got all the information my agent might need organized in .md files and each bit of information is coded so the agent can find that specific bit of info with loading the entire file into it's context.  I'm talking design stuff, engine documentation, I even curated game development philosophy/  It's all in layers of .md files with a router file at the top.  

I prefer to use the top model (fable, sol, opus) at high or very high effort to avoid mistakes that require another round to fix.  Every time you prompt the AI, it loads the entire previous context, wasting tokens.  I try to give it long horizon tasks , and I have Claude use those little question pop-ups if it needs me to do something, like restart the engine or something.
